squeeze/recall: A sequence-to-sequence model reads, je suis étudiant, with an encoder, and writes, I am a student, with a decoder. Everything it read reaches the decoder through one vector: the encoder's final state.
squeeze/long: That vector has a fixed size. Three words or fifty, the whole sentence must squeeze into the same few numbers, and long sentences came out translated worse.
squeeze/bahdanau: In 2014, Dzmitry Bahdanau, Kyunghyun Cho and Yoshua Bengio called that fixed-length vector a bottleneck. Their fix: let the decoder look back at every encoder state, not just the last.
squeeze/keep: The encoder already makes one state per input word as it reads. Keep them all, and call them h j: the state after word j, counting from zero.
look/need: To write its first word, I, the decoder needs je far more than suis or étudiant. So it needs a way to score each encoder state for the word at hand.
look/arrows: Picture the states as arrows. Real ones hold hundreds of numbers; these hold two, so they fit on a page.
look/q: The decoder has a state of its own, an arrow too. Call it q, for query: what the decoder is looking for right now.
look/score: Score each encoder state by its dot product with q, which is big when two arrows point the same way. This q lies along the first axis, so each score is how far a state reaches along it: two for je, one for étudiant, and zero for suis, at a right angle.
look/sj: Those are the scores, s j equals q dot h j: biggest for the state that lines up best with q.
look/luong: In 2015, Minh-Thang Luong, Hieu Pham and Christopher Manning found that this plain dot product works well as the score. The first attention model had used a small learned network instead.
look/weights: Softmax turns the scores into weights, positive and adding up to one: about zero point six seven, zero point zero nine and zero point two four. The highest score still gets the most.
look/alpha: These are the attention weights, alpha j: how much attention the decoder pays to each input word. The word comes from Bahdanau's paper: the decoder decides which parts of the sentence to pay attention to.
mix/blend: Now blend the states into one vector, each counting as much as its weight says: shrink every arrow by its weight, then add them up.
mix/scale: Je's state, two, one, times zero point six seven, shrinks to one point three four, zero point six seven. The other two, with small weights, shrink almost away.
mix/add: Add them by laying the arrows tip to tail. The sum ends at one point five eight, zero point six one: mostly je, a little of the rest.
mix/context: This weighted sum is called the context vector, the sum over j of alpha j times h j: the part of the input that matters for the word being written now.
mix/use: The decoder reads the context vector along with its own state, and predicts its next word: I.
every/again: At the next step the decoder's state has moved on, so q points somewhere new, and the weights shift: for the words am and a, mostly to suis; for student, to étudiant.
every/grid: Stack each step's weights as a row, and you see which input words each output word drew on. Bahdanau's paper drew grids like this, and called them alignments: which words line up across the two languages.
every/free: Nothing has to squeeze through one fixed-size vector any more: at every step, the decoder can read every input state directly.
